claims.text: The baseline refractory HEA has a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution microstructure with minimal intrinsic precipitates.
The intervention adds 2 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles to the baseline refractory HEA.
Powder mixing followed by spark plasma sintering can produce a fine, uniform dispersion of the Y2O3 nanoparticles.
The intervention produces nanoscale Y2O3 particles along grain boundaries.
The intervention produces nanoscale Y2O3 particles within the alloy matrix.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening at elevated temperature.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the Y2O3 dispersion retards creep.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the Y2O3 dispersion improves elevated-temperature yield strength.
The low nanoparticle fraction minimizes the effect of the addition on alloy density.
The low nanoparticle fraction minimizes the effect of the addition on room-temperature ductility.
At approximately 1100°C, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have at least 15% greater yield strength than the baseline refractory HEA.
At approximately 1100°C under constant-load creep testing, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have a statistically significant reduction in creep rate relative to the baseline.
The Y2O3 addition will cause negligible changes in room-temperature mechanical properties.
The Y2O3 addition will increase density by less than 2% relative to the baseline.
The predicted beneficial effect requires a uniform nanoparticle dispersion.
Excessive nanoparticle clustering could negate the predicted benefits.
High-temperature interfacial reactions between Y2O3 and the alloy matrix could alter phase stability and negate the predicted benefits.
The effects may depend on the refractory HEA composition.
The effects may be limited to processing windows that avoid nanoparticle agglomeration.
